pages.summary: A table whose rows are points in time.
body: Each row has a time, a datetime or a duration: given as a vector, or made regular from a sample rate or a time step (from a start time, 0 seconds unless given). `TT.Time` (or the first dimension's name) holds the times; `TT(t, :)` picks rows by their times and `TT(timerange(t1, t2), :)` the rows between two. `retime`, `synchronize` and `lag` work on the times; anything a table does, a timetable does too. `TT.Properties` also has `RowTimes`, `StartTime`, `SampleRate` and `TimeStep`.

pages.summary: The rows of a timetable between two times.
body: Used as the row index, `TT(timerange(t1, t2), :)` keeps the rows from t1 up to but not including t2; `'closed'`, `'open'` and `'openleft'` include or leave out the ends otherwise. The times are datetimes or durations, as the row times are.
syntax: With the ends included or left out.

examples.title: A morning's readings

pages.summary: Timetables from tables and matrices, and back to tables.
body: `table2timetable` takes the first datetime or duration variable as the row times (or the variable or times named by `'RowTimes'`); `timetable2table` makes the row times the first variable again; `array2timetable` makes each column of a matrix a variable, at the times given or regular ones.
syntax: The first time variable as row times.

examples.title: A log becoming a timetable
examples.code:
T = table(datetime(2026, 11, [3; 4; 5]), [12; 15; 11], 'VariableNames', {'Day', 'Visits'});
TT = table2timetable(T)
timetable2table(TT)
A = array2timetable([1 2; 3 4; 5 6], 'TimeStep', minutes(15), 'VariableNames', {'In', 'Out'})

pages.summary: Timetables at new row times: filled in, or put together over intervals; and several side by side at common times.
body: `retime` takes a timetable to new times: a vector, a regular step (`'hourly'`, `'daily'` and the like, or `'regular'` with `'TimeStep'` or `'SampleRate'`). Each new time either takes a value filled in (`'fillwithmissing'`, `'previous'`, `'nearest'`, `'linear'`, `'spline'` ...) or puts together the rows from it up to the next (`'mean'`, `'sum'`, `'max'`, `'count'`, a function ...). `synchronize` puts timetables side by side at the union of their times (or `'intersection'`, `'first'`, a step), each filled or put together the same way.
syntax: At a step of a duration.

pages.summary: Whether a timetable's times step evenly, and its data moved by rows.
body: `isregular` is true when the row times step evenly, giving the step; with a calendar unit (`'months'`, `'days'` ...), when they step by whole units of it. `lag` moves the data n rows later (1 unless given; negative moves earlier), the times staying where they are and missing values where there is nothing.
syntax: The data moved n rows later.

pages.summary: A function applied to each variable of a table, or to each row.
body: `varfun` calls the function on each variable (or `'InputVariables'`), giving a table of results named after the function and the variable (`mean_x`); with `'GroupingVariables'`, once per group, with each group's size in `GroupCount`. `rowfun` calls it on each row, the row's variables as its inputs; with grouping variables, once per group with the group's rows. `'OutputFormat'` gives an array (`'uniform'`) or a cell array instead of a table.
syntax: On some variables, the results named.

examples.title: A function of each row
examples.code:
T = table([1; 2; 4], [10; 30; 60], 'VariableNames', {'x', 'y'});
rowfun(@(x, y) y/x, T, 'InputVariables', {'x', 'y'}, 'OutputVariableNames', 'ratio')

pages.summary: Statistics of a table's variables for each group of rows, and how many rows each group has.
body: `groupsummary` gives a row per group (sorted), its size in `GroupCount`, and each method of each data variable named `method_variable`: `'mean'`, `'sum'`, `'min'`, `'max'`, `'range'`, `'median'`, `'mode'`, `'var'`, `'std'`, `'nnz'`, `'numel'`, `'nummissing'`, `'all'` or a function; missing values are left out. Without data variables, every numeric variable that does not group. `groupcounts` gives the groups with `GroupCount` and `Percent`; for an array, the counts, the groups and the percentages.

pages.summary: Each group's data transformed, and the rows of groups that pass a test.
body: `grouptransform` replaces each data variable by its transform within each group (`'zscore'`, `'norm'`, `'meancenter'`, `'rescale'`, `'meanfill'`, `'linearfill'`, or a function of a column), or with `'ReplaceValues', false` adds the results as new variables. `groupfilter` keeps the rows of the groups for which a function of the group's column is true (a single value for the whole group, or one for each row).
syntax: G = grouptransform(T, groupvars, method, datavars, 'ReplaceValues', false)
The rows of the groups that pass.

pages.summary: A table of a statistic for each row group and column group.
body: The values of one variable become columns (`'Columns'`), another's the rows (`'Rows'`), and each cell holds a statistic of the rows that fall there: the count (without `'DataVariable'`), or the `'Method'` of the data variable (`'sum'` unless given; `'mean'`, `'max'`, a function ...).
syntax: P = pivot(T, 'Columns', cvar, 'Rows', rvar, 'DataVariable', dvar, 'Method', m)

pages.summary: The k rows that sort first.
body: The k largest rows by the columns (or variables) given, ties broken by the next ones; `'ascend'` for the smallest. The second output gives the rows' places.
syntax: The k largest rows of a matrix.

pages.summary: Variables of a table stacked into one, and a variable spread into several.
body: `stack` makes a row for each row and stacked variable: the other variables repeated, an indicator of which variable (categorical), and its value. `unstack` goes the other way: a row for each group (of the other variables, or `'GroupingVariables'`) and a variable for each value of the indicator; several values in one place are summed (or given to `'AggregationFunction'`), none gives a missing value.

pages.summary: Two tables joined by their keys: the matching rows only, or every row with missing values where there is no match.
body: The keys are the variables of the same name unless given (`'Keys'`, or `'LeftKeys'` and `'RightKeys'`). `innerjoin` keeps the rows whose keys are in both; `outerjoin` keeps all of them (`'Type'` `'full'`, or `'left'` or `'right'` for one side's), the other side's variables missing where nothing matches; `'MergeKeys'` makes each pair of keys one variable. The result is sorted by the keys; the outputs ia and ib say which rows of each input made each row.

pages.summary: Tables read from text files and spreadsheets, and written to them.
body: `readtable` reads .csv, .txt and .dat files (and .xlsx spreadsheets): the first row names the variables, and each column becomes numbers, datetimes or text. Options set the delimiter, header lines, row names, sheet and text type. `writetable` writes a table the same way (comma-separated unless `'Delimiter'` says, a spreadsheet for .xlsx), and `writetimetable` a timetable, its row times the first column.
syntax: With the delimiter and header lines given.
